# Web Platform: css.md

Self-contained. The skill's rules, then this topic, then anything it relies on from other skills.

## Skill rules

How I build for the web: browser-native HTML, CSS and JS, the Next.js App Router, Astro, and Supabase auth. Plus the accessibility, performance, security and visual details that separate hand-built work from component-library output.

Evergreen browsers only. No legacy prefixes. No polyfills for anything above 95% support. Mobile-first: build for a mid-range Android phone on a cell network, not a desktop monitor.

JavaScript causes most performance problems. Load less of it. Move logic to the server. If CSS or HTML can do it, that's where it goes.

### Rules for Every Web Task

**CSS layer order.** Declare it once at the top of the root stylesheet. A later layer beats an earlier one regardless of specificity:

```css
@layer reset, base, tokens, components, utilities, overrides;
```

**Tokens live in one `:root` block.** Color, spacing, type, radius, shadow and motion all reference custom properties named after the design file's token paths (`--color-semantic-text-primary`). No raw values in component rules. Colors are `oklch()`.

**Animate `transform` and `opacity`.** They composite. `width`, `height`, `top`, `left`, `margin` and `padding` run layout every frame. Motion values come from the design or `motion-design`. Don't invent them. Write motion inside `prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference`.

**Server Components are the Next.js default.** `"use client"` only for state, effects, event handlers or browser APIs. Keep it at the leaves.

**Request APIs are async.** Await `cookies()`, `headers()`, `draftMode()`, `params` and `searchParams`. Request interception lives in `proxy.ts`.

**Caching is explicit.** With Cache Components on, nothing is cached unless it's marked `"use cache"`. Anything that reads request data or uncached data sits inside `<Suspense>`.

**Every input has a `<label>`.** Validate on the server, always. Client-side validation is UX, not security.

**Lane rules.** Vercel is frontend only. Publishable key, RLS enforced, the secret key never touches it. The publishable key goes through `@supabase/ssr` with the user's cookie session, and RLS via `auth.uid()` is the security boundary. A query that needs the secret key belongs on Railway behind an API endpoint. Every Server Function verifies the user itself, because it's reachable by direct POST.

**Support policy.** Baseline widely available: use it freely. Newly available: use it, with an `@supports` or feature-detected fallback only where a miss would break function, not polish. Limited availability: progressive enhancement only. Check `reference/browser-compatibility.md` before reaching for anything newer than container queries.

### Common Mistakes

| Mistake | Why it's wrong |
| --- | --- |
| JS-computed sizing or scroll listeners where container queries or scroll-driven animations do the job | Layout reads force reflow on the main thread |
| `outline: none` with no replacement | Fails WCAG 2.4.7 |
| `user-scalable=no` or `maximum-scale=1` | Blocks zoom. WCAG 1.4.4 |
| `html { font-size: <16px }` or the `62.5%` rem hack | Overrides the user's font-size preference |
| Placeholder text as a label | Disappears on input and isn't a dependable accessible name |
| Infinite scroll with no alternative | Keyboard and screen-reader users lose the footer and their place |
| `loading="lazy"` on the LCP image, or no `fetchpriority="high"` on it | Directly hurts LCP |
| `revalidateTag("tag")` with one argument | Type error. Pass a profile: `revalidateTag("tag", "max")` |
| `priority` on `next/image` | Not the prop. The LCP image takes `fetchPriority="high"` with `loading="eager"` |
| Plain `@supabase/supabase-js` client in server code on Vercel | No cookie session, no refresh. Use `@supabase/ssr` |
| `getSession()` to authorize on the server | Reads the cookie without verifying it. Use `getClaims()` |
| `proxy.ts` as the only auth check | A matcher change silently removes it. Check in the page and the Server Function too |
| Per-user data inside a shared `"use cache"` | Replayed with no RLS check |
| `z` from `astro:content`, or `entry.render()` | `z` is from `astro/zod`. `render()` is imported from `astro:content` |

All CSS is custom. I don't use Tailwind or any framework, and no preprocessor unless the project already has one. Support status for every feature is in `browser-compatibility.md`. Sections marked **Newer** aren't widely available yet, so that file's policy applies.

Who owns what:

- **Token names** come from `figma-design-system/reference/token-architecture.md`. It's the Figma path with slashes turned into hyphens: `color/semantic/text/primary` is `--color-semantic-text-primary`. Names in code and in the design file match exactly.

- **Motion tokens and CSS motion technique** come from `motion-design` (`reference/cross-platform-tokens.md`, `reference/web-css-transitions.md`). Samples here use its names (`--duration-fast`, `--ease-enter`) and never define values.

### Layers and Tokens

```css
@layer reset, base, tokens, components, utilities, overrides;
```

Each layer beats the ones before it regardless of specificity. `!important` is never needed to win a specificity fight. Unlayered styles beat every layer, so import third-party CSS into one: `@import url("vendor.css") layer(reset);`.

All tokens live in one `:root` block. Primitives hold raw values. Semantic tokens alias primitives, and components use the semantic ones. `light-dark()` keeps both color schemes in that one block. No second block inside a media query.

```css
@layer tokens {
    :root {
        color-scheme: light dark;

        --color-primitive-gray-50: oklch(98% 0 0);
        --color-primitive-gray-900: oklch(15% 0 0);
        --color-primitive-blue-300: oklch(78% 0.12 260);
        --color-primitive-blue-500: oklch(60% 0.2 260);
        --spacing-2: 0.5rem;
        --spacing-4: 1rem;
        --radius-md: 0.5rem;

        --color-semantic-background-primary: light-dark(var(--color-primitive-gray-50), var(--color-primitive-gray-900));
        --color-semantic-text-primary: light-dark(var(--color-primitive-gray-900), var(--color-primitive-gray-50));
        --color-semantic-interactive-primary: light-dark(var(--color-primitive-blue-500), var(--color-primitive-blue-300));
    }

    /* Manual theme switch: flip the scheme, not the tokens */
    :root[data-theme="light"] { color-scheme: light; }
    :root[data-theme="dark"] { color-scheme: dark; }
}

@layer components {
    .button {
        background: var(--color-semantic-interactive-primary);
        padding: var(--spacing-2) var(--spacing-4);
        border-radius: var(--radius-md);
    }
}
```

Those values show the shape. Real ones come from the design file and `color-system`. A component rule never contains a raw color, length, radius, shadow, duration or easing.

Nesting is native. Keep it to two levels. Deeper nesting rebuilds the specificity problems layers exist to end.

### Color

`oklch(lightness chroma hue)`. Equal lightness steps look equal, and changing lightness doesn't drift the hue. HSL can't promise either. Derive variants, don't hand-pick them:

```css
:root {
    --color-semantic-interactive-primary-hover:
        oklch(from var(--color-semantic-interactive-primary) calc(l - 0.08) c h);
    --color-semantic-interactive-primary-subtle:
        color-mix(in oklch, var(--color-semantic-interactive-primary) 20%, transparent);
}
```

`contrast-color()` (**Newer**) only picks black or white. Anything beyond that is `color-system`'s job, along with palette generation, contrast math and gamut clamping.

### @scope

**Newer.** Scopes a component's rules to its subtree, with an optional lower boundary so they stop at nested components. It replaces BEM naming and CSS-in-JS scoping.

```css
@scope (.card) to (.card-slot) {
    :scope { padding: var(--spacing-4); }
    img { border-radius: var(--radius-md); }
}
```

`img` matches images in `.card`, but not inside a `.card-slot` within it.

### Container and Style Queries

Media queries are for page layout and user preferences. Component layout uses container queries, because a component doesn't know how wide its slot is.

```css
.card-wrapper { container: card / inline-size; }

.card {
    display: grid;

    @container card (inline-size >= 25rem) {
        grid-template-columns: 12rem 1fr;
    }
}
```

**Newer: style queries.** A parent sets a custom property once and descendants respond. No modifier class on each child. Only custom properties can be queried.

```css
.card-wrapper { --variant: compact; }

@container style(--variant: compact) {
    .card-meta { display: none; }
}
```

When cards in a row have to align their internal rows, use `grid-template-rows: subgrid`. Don't equalize heights in JS.

### :has()

```css
.field:has(input:user-invalid) { color: var(--color-semantic-status-error); }

/* Lock page scroll while a modal dialog is open */
html:has(dialog:modal) { overflow: hidden; }
```

Use `:user-invalid`, not `:invalid`. It only matches after the user has interacted, so an empty required field isn't red on load.

### Fluid Type and Viewport Units

```css
:root {
    --typography-size-title-lg: clamp(1.75rem, 1.3rem + 2.5vw, 3rem);
}
```

The preferred value always includes a `rem` term. A size in `vw` alone ignores zoom and the user's font-size setting, and fails WCAG 1.4.4. Same reason font sizes are never plain `px`.

`100vh` is the largest viewport on mobile. It overflows whenever browser chrome is visible. Use `100dvh` for full-height sections, `svh` for content that can't be cut off, `lvh` only for decorative backgrounds.

### Anchor Positioning

**Newer.** The native replacement for JS positioning libraries in tooltips, menus and popovers.

```css
.trigger { anchor-name: --trigger; }

.menu {
    position: absolute;
    position-anchor: --trigger;
    position-area: block-end span-inline-end;
    margin-block-start: var(--spacing-2);
    position-try-fallbacks: flip-block, flip-inline;
}
```

`position-area` places the element on a 3x3 grid around the anchor. `position-try-fallbacks` flips it when it would overflow. Name the anchor explicitly, even for a popover and its invoker. Implicit anchoring isn't consistent across engines. Keep a plain positioned fallback outside `@supports (position-area: block-end)`. The pattern is in `browser-compatibility.md`.

### Motion Rules

Technique and tokens are in `motion-design/reference/web-css-transitions.md`: entry and exit with `@starting-style`, intrinsic-size animation, scroll-driven animations, view transitions. Don't write a second version here. The web rules on top of it:

- Motion is opt-in. Write it inside `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference)`, so the default state is the finished, readable one.
- The un-animated state is always complete. An element that starts at `opacity: 0` and needs an animation to appear is invisible where the feature is missing.
- Keep scroll-driven animations inside `@supports (animation-timeline: view())` until `browser-compatibility.md` lists them as widely available.
- Where a browser can't transition `display`, exit animations built on `allow-discrete` are skipped. That's acceptable. Don't add JS to paper over it.
- A disclosure animates height with `grid-template-rows: 0fr` to `1fr`. `interpolate-size` replaces that only once it's in every browser.
- Scroll-driven animations scrub with the scroll position. For an animation that plays once when an element enters the viewport, IntersectionObserver plus a class is still the cross-browser tool.
- Each `view-transition-name` is unique at the moment of the snapshot. In React use `<ViewTransition>` (`nextjs.md`), not `document.startViewTransition`. Cross-document transitions fall back to a normal navigation where unsupported.

### CSS Instead of JavaScript

- `text-wrap: balance` on headings, `text-wrap: pretty` on body copy.
- `field-sizing: content` grows a `<textarea>` with its content. **Newer.**
- `sibling-index()` for staggered delays without inline styles. **Newer.**
- `scrollbar-gutter: stable` stops the shift when a scrollbar appears.
- `scroll-padding-block-start` on the scroller keeps anchored and focused content clear of a sticky header.
- `@property` gives a custom property a type, which makes it animatable (gradient angles, numeric counters).

### Performance

Animate `transform` (or `translate`, `scale`, `rotate`) and `opacity`. They composite without layout or paint. `width`, `height`, `top`, `left`, `margin` and `padding` run layout every frame.

```css
.card {
    transition: translate var(--duration-fast) var(--ease-enter);

    @media (hover: hover) {
        &:hover { translate: 0 calc(-1 * var(--motion-distance-sm)); }
    }
}
```

One exception: the disclosure above. Its content has to push other content down, and it's small, user-triggered and short.

- `will-change` only on an element about to animate, removed afterwards. Left on, it pins a layer in memory.
- `content-visibility: auto` with `contain-intrinsic-size` skips rendering for long off-screen sections.
- `filter`, `backdrop-filter` and `mix-blend-mode` are cheap to write and expensive to paint over large areas. Test on a mid-range phone.

What this file relies on from other skills, copied in so nothing needs looking up.

### From figma-design-system: Token Architecture

This file defines token naming for the whole skill library. `color-system`, `web-platform`, `apple-platform`, `android-platform`, `visual-styles`, and `motion-design` all follow it. Values aren't defined here. Each family names the skill that has its values.

##### Contents
- [Three Tiers](#three-tiers)
- [Token Families](#token-families)
- [Conversion Rule](#conversion-rule)
- [Platform-Supplied Tokens](#platform-supplied-tokens)
- [Variable Collections in Figma](#variable-collections-in-figma)
- [Light and Dark Modes](#light-and-dark-modes)
- [Typography](#typography)
- [Spacing and Radius](#spacing-and-radius)

##### Three Tiers

Never apply a primitive directly to a component. Alias through a semantic token.

**Tier 1: Primitive.** Raw values, never applied directly. `color/primitive/warm-200`, `spacing/primitive/16`, `radius/primitive/8`.

**Tier 2: Semantic.** Meaning and intent. This is what gets applied. `color/semantic/background/primary`, `spacing/5`, `radius/md`.

**Tier 3: Component.** Enterprise scale only. `button/primary/background/default`, `card/border`.

Semantic tokens are the endpoint for most projects. Component tokens only pay off with multiple teams and strict governance. Three tiers is the max. Two is often enough.

##### Token Families

Figma paths are lowercase, slash-separated, kebab-case inside a segment. Every token in every skill is one of these.

| Family | Figma path | Names in use | Values come from |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Color, primitive | `color/primitive/<name>` | The palette name verbatim: `swiss-red`, `warm-200`, `cool-900`. A project ramp is `<hue>-<step>`, steps 50 to 950 | `color-system` (reference/palette.md) |
| Color, semantic | `color/semantic/<group>/<role>` | Groups: `background`, `text`, `border`, `status`, `interactive`, `accent`. Roles below | `color-system` (semantic mappings) |
| Color, component | `<component>/<variant>/<property>/<state>` | `button/primary/background/hover`, `card/background`. Drop segments that don't apply | Aliases of semantic tokens only |
| Spacing | `spacing/<step>`, primitive `spacing/primitive/<px>` | Steps `1` to `12` | This file |
| Radius | `radius/<size>`, primitive `radius/primitive/<px>` | `none`, `xs`, `sm`, `md`, `lg`, `xl`, `2xl`, `sheet`, `pill` | This file |
| Size | `size/<name>` | Fixed dimensions: `size/target-min`, `size/header-height` | Platform skills |
| Stacking | `z/<layer>` | One token per layer: `z/modal`, `z/toast` | Platform skills |
| Effect | `effect/<kind>/<step>` | `effect/blur/md`, `effect/glow/radius` | `visual-styles`, platform skills |
| Shadow | `shadow/<name>` | A whole shadow recipe: `shadow/raised`, `shadow/inset`, `shadow/hard-sm` | `visual-styles`, platform skills |
| Typography | `typography/family/<name>`, `typography/size/<role>`, `typography/weight/<name>`, `typography/leading/<name>`, `typography/tracking/<name>` | Below | Platform skills (sizes), this file (names) |
| Motion | `motion/spring/<name>`, `motion/duration/<name>`, `motion/ease/<name>`, `motion/distance/<size>` | Listed in `motion-design` (reference/cross-platform-tokens.md), not here | `motion-design` |
| Glass | `glass/<parameter>/<variant>` | Figma-only, in [liquid-glass.md](../figma-design-system/liquid-glass.md) | No code equivalent. The system draws glass |

Semantic color roles:

```
color/semantic/background/primary | secondary | elevated
color/semantic/text/primary | secondary | disabled
color/semantic/border/default | focus
color/semantic/status/success | warning | error
color/semantic/interactive/primary | primary-hover | primary-pressed
color/semantic/accent/primary | secondary | tertiary
```

The six groups are fixed. `accent` is decorative brand color that isn't interactive. New roles go inside a group (`text/inverse`, `status/info`). A state is a suffix on its role (`-hover`, `-pressed`, `-disabled`), not a new segment. Name by meaning, never by appearance: `interactive/primary`, not `purple-500`.

A style in `visual-styles` can declare extra style-local tokens. They follow the same families and the same conversion rule.

##### Conversion Rule

One Figma path gives every platform's name mechanically. Nothing is abbreviated, reordered, or dropped.

- **Figma:** as written.
- **CSS:** `--`, then every segment joined with `-`.
- **Swift:** every segment but the last is a PascalCase namespace. The last is lowerCamelCase.
- **Kotlin:** same as Swift, on the project's token object.

| Figma | CSS | Swift and Kotlin |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `color/semantic/background/primary` | `--color-semantic-background-primary` | `Color.Semantic.Background.primary` |
| `color/primitive/warm-200` | `--color-primitive-warm-200` | `Color.Primitive.warm200` |
| `spacing/5` | `--spacing-5` | `Spacing.s5` |
| `radius/2xl` | `--radius-2xl` | `Radius.r2xl` |
| `size/target-min` | `--size-target-min` | `Size.targetMin` |
| `z/modal` | `--z-modal` | `Z.modal` |
| `effect/blur/md` | `--effect-blur-md` | `Effect.Blur.md` |
| `typography/size/display-lg` | `--typography-size-display-lg` | `Typography.Size.displayLg` |

Hyphenated names become lowerCamelCase in Swift and Kotlin: `expo-out` is `expoOut`.

**A last segment that starts with a digit** can't be a Swift or Kotlin identifier. It takes the lowercase first letter of its parent segment: `spacing/5` → `Spacing.s5`, `radius/2xl` → `Radius.r2xl`. CSS needs no prefix.

Motion has two exceptions. They're the only ones.

| Figma | CSS | Swift | Kotlin |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `motion/spring/snappy` | `--spring-snappy` | `Motion.Spring.snappy` | `Motion.Spring.snappy()` |
| `motion/duration/standard` | `--duration-standard` | `Motion.Duration.standard` | `Motion.Duration.standard` |
| `motion/ease/expo-out` | `--ease-expo-out` | `Motion.Ease.expoOut` and `Motion.Curve.expoOut` | `Motion.Ease.expoOut` |
| `motion/distance/sm` | `--motion-distance-sm` | `Motion.Distance.sm` | `Motion.Distance.sm` |

- **CSS drops the `motion` segment** for springs, durations, and eases. `motion/distance` keeps it.
- **In Swift, `motion/ease/<name>` gives two members.** `Motion.Ease.<name>` is the ready-to-use Animation, the curve at its default duration. `Motion.Curve.<name>` is the bare curve.

Kotlin follows the rule with nested objects. Springs are generic functions, so they're called: `Motion.Spring.snappy()`.

If a codebase already ships tokens under other names, the code's names win. Rename the Figma variable so it converts to them. The rule decides names for anything new.

**Code syntax carries the name.** Every Figma variable has a per-platform code syntax field (Web, Android, iOS). Dev Mode and the MCP read tools show it. Set it on every variable, for every platform the project targets, to the literal string a developer types: `var(--color-semantic-background-primary)` for Web, with the `var()` wrapper, and `Color.Semantic.Background.primary` for iOS. A variable with the right path and an empty or wrong code syntax fails the token-name gate.

##### Platform-Supplied Tokens

Where the platform already provides the token, don't redefine it in code. The Figma variable keeps its semantic path, because one file serves several platforms. The platform's own name goes in that platform's code syntax field.

| Figma token | SwiftUI | Compose (Material 3) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `color/semantic/background/primary` | `Color(.systemBackground)` | `MaterialTheme.colorScheme.surface` |
| `color/semantic/background/secondary` | `Color(.secondarySystemBackground)` | `MaterialTheme.colorScheme.surfaceContainer` |
| `color/semantic/text/primary` | `Color(.label)` | `MaterialTheme.colorScheme.onSurface` |
| `color/semantic/text/secondary` | `Color(.secondaryLabel)` | `MaterialTheme.colorScheme.onSurfaceVariant` |
| `color/semantic/border/default` | `Color(.separator)` | `MaterialTheme.colorScheme.outline` |
| `color/semantic/interactive/primary` | `Color.accentColor` | `MaterialTheme.colorScheme.primary` |
| `color/semantic/status/error` | project token | `MaterialTheme.colorScheme.error` |

Use the platform token when it covers the case. Project tokens fill the gaps: brand colors, product-specific surfaces, anything the system palette doesn't have. The full platform sets are in `apple-platform` and `android-platform`.

##### Variable Collections in Figma

Four collections, kept separate.

**Primitives.** All raw values. One mode. No light/dark here.

**Semantic Color.** Modes: Light, Dark. Every semantic color aliases a primitive. Switching modes swaps the alias target, not the token name.

**Semantic Spacing, Radius, Motion.** Number variables, one mode. Add modes only for density variants. If the file uses Figma Motion, durations and easing curves are timing and easing variables, not plain numbers.

**Typography.** String variables for font family and weight, number variables for size and line height. One family variable retypes the whole system.

On every variable:
- **Scope** it to where it can be used. A text color to text fills, a radius to corner radius. Primitives are scoped to nothing, so they can't be applied directly. That enforces the tier rule.
- **Code syntax** per target platform.

**Mode limits change what can be built.** Light and Dark fit every paid plan. Before designing a collection around many modes (brand × theme × density × contrast), check the per-plan limit in [platform-status.md](../figma-design-system/platform-status.md). Multi-brand theming through extended collections is Enterprise only. On other plans, multi-brand is separate brand collections aliased by the semantic layer.

##### Light and Dark Modes

Both modes live in the Semantic Color collection. Every token has a Light value and a Dark value, and both alias primitives. Never put a raw hex value in a semantic token.

```
color/semantic/background/primary
  Light: → color/primitive/warm-200
  Dark:  → color/primitive/cool-900
```

Which primitive each role aliases in each mode is `color-system`'s call, or the project palette's. Not this file's.

Design in dark mode first. If it works in dark, it almost always works in light. The reverse doesn't hold.

Set the mode on each screen's top frame. Layers default to Auto and inherit from the nearest parent with a mode set, so nothing inside a component carries an explicit mode. For review, place each screen twice, one frame Light and one Dark, side by side.

##### Typography

```
typography/family/sans      → "SF Pro" (iOS), "Roboto Flex" (Android), project typeface (Web)
typography/family/mono      → "SF Mono", "Roboto Mono", project mono

typography/size/display-lg  → 40
typography/size/display-sm  → 32
typography/size/title-lg    → 28
typography/size/title-md    → 22
typography/size/title-sm    → 20
typography/size/headline    → 17
typography/size/body        → 17
typography/size/callout     → 16
typography/size/subhead     → 15
typography/size/footnote    → 13
typography/size/caption     → 12

typography/weight/regular | medium | semibold | bold   → "Regular", "Medium", "Semibold", "Bold"
typography/leading/tight | normal | relaxed            → 1.2, 1.5, 1.7
```

These sizes are iOS and iPadOS at the default Dynamic Type size, from `apple-platform` (reference/color-typography.md). `title-lg`, `title-md`, `title-sm` are Apple's title, title2, title3. macOS, Android, and Web sizes come from their platform skills. Where they differ, the Typography collection gets one mode per platform, not a second set of names.

One text style per semantic role, not per size:

```
Display Large / Small    hero content, section headers
Title Large / Medium / Small    screen titles, card headers, subheaders
Headline                 emphasized body
Body                     primary reading content
Callout                  supporting text
Subheadline              metadata
Footnote                 timestamps, legal
Caption                  image captions, form help text
Label Large / Medium / Small    button labels, tags, badges
```

Text styles reference the typography variables. Ask for that binding explicitly and read it back afterwards. The plugin's library-generation path creates text styles with literal values unless told otherwise, and a style with raw numbers inside looks correct until the typeface changes. The font has to be uploaded to the Figma account. One installed only locally isn't available to an MCP session.

##### Spacing and Radius

8pt grid. All spacing tokens are multiples of 4, preferring multiples of 8. Apply them as number variables to padding and gap in Auto Layout frames. No hardcoded values.

```
spacing/1 → 2     spacing/5 → 16 (base)    spacing/9  → 40
spacing/2 → 4     spacing/6 → 20           spacing/10 → 48
spacing/3 → 8     spacing/7 → 24           spacing/11 → 64
spacing/4 → 12    spacing/8 → 32           spacing/12 → 80
```

```
radius/none → 0    radius/md → 12    radius/2xl   → 28
radius/xs   → 4    radius/lg → 16    radius/sheet → 34
radius/sm   → 8    radius/xl → 24    radius/pill  → capsule
```

`radius/pill` is a capsule, not a number. In code it's the platform's capsule shape (`.capsule` in SwiftUI), never a large radius. Figma needs a number, so the variable holds any value larger than half the tallest pill in the file. That number is a Figma artifact. It never goes in code syntax.

On iOS, `radius/2xl` is the floating-panel radius (`Radius.r2xl`, 28) and `radius/sheet` is the sheet radius (`Radius.sheet`, 34). Cards aren't glass. On Android, `radius/md` is Material's medium shape (12dp) and `radius/2xl` its extraLarge (28dp). The full shape scale is in `android-platform`.

### From color-system: Palette: Named Primitives

All 73 primitives with hex and OKLCH values. Hex is the source of truth. The OKLCH column is the same sRGB color, precise enough to round-trip to the identical 8-bit hex, so the two are interchangeable in CSS. Use OKLCH on web, hex or component values elsewhere.

Every value is inside sRGB. Wide-gamut and per-platform token setup are in [implementation.md](../color-system/implementation.md). Semantic roles, pairing rules, and contrast are in [../SKILL.md](../color-system/index.md).

##### Swiss International Style

Derived from the poster work of Josef Muller-Brockmann, Armin Hofmann, Theo Ballmer, Max Bill, and others working in the International Typographic Style from the 1950s through the 1970s. They were used in deliberate, limited combinations, rarely more than two or three per composition.

The Swiss style used color functionally: one bold color as an accent against black and white, or two carefully chosen primaries in contrast. The colors are saturated but not garish. They read as strong and precise, not loud.

| `swiss-red-warm` | `#E63229` | `oklch(60.33% 0.2164 28.55)` | Warmer, more orange-leaning variant. Muller-Brockmann road safety series. |

##### Bauhaus Primary Palette

From Johannes Itten's color theory. Itten taught the Bauhaus preliminary course from 1919 to 1923 and published the system in *The Art of Color* (1961). The school itself ran until 1933. These colors are the purest articulation of primary-triad thinking in 20th-century design, and they shaped Swiss Style directly.

Itten's system: three primaries at maximum saturation, always used in relationship to each other and to the neutrals black and white. Bauhaus white is `swiss-pure-white`.

| Token | Hex | OKLCH | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `bauhaus-red` | `#C8302A` | `oklch(54.87% 0.1896 27.76)` | Itten primary red. Neither blue-shifted nor orange-shifted. |
| `bauhaus-yellow` | `#E8C018` | `oklch(81.91% 0.1639 93.23)` | Itten primary yellow. Warm gold-yellow, not pure lemon. |
| `bauhaus-blue` | `#1E3878` | `oklch(35.96% 0.1142 264.64)` | Itten primary blue. Deep cobalt, not navy and not sky. |
| `bauhaus-black` | `#000000` | `oklch(0.00% 0 0)` | Pure black. Itten used it as a structural color, not just text. |
| `bauhaus-gray` | `#808080` | `oklch(59.99% 0 0)` | Neutral mid-gray. Itten's intermediate between black and white. |

Secondaries (Itten's mixed secondaries):

| Token | Hex | OKLCH | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

| `bauhaus-green` | `#2A7A3A` | `oklch(51.49% 0.1247 147.26)` | Yellow + Blue. Forest, not lime. |
| `bauhaus-violet` | `#5C2080` | `oklch(38.46% 0.1553 309.43)` | Red + Blue. Deep purple-violet. |

##### Source Notes

**Swiss International Style colors** come from the posters: Muller-Brockmann's Musica Viva and road safety series, Hofmann's Basel Theater posters, Ballmer's Norm poster (1928), and related works held by MoMA and the Museum of Design Zurich. Fabian Burghardt's Swiss Style Color Picker (fabianburghardt.de/swisscolors, 2015) systematized these combinations, and the colors here line up with his. The hex values are a digitization of ink on paper. They're a faithful approximation, not a colorimetric match.

**Bauhaus primary palette** values come from Hue Atlas (hueatlas.com) and its reading of Itten's *The Art of Color* and archival originals. `#C8302A` / `#E8C018` / `#1E3878` sit in the middle of the range across those sources, allowing for the gamut difference between lithographic inks and RGB displays. Same caveat: ink to RGB is approximate.

### From color-system: Implementing the Palette

How to write these primitives and semantic roles as tokens on each platform, and what the current color features do and don't solve. General color technique is in the `web-platform`, `apple-platform`, and `android-platform` skills. This is the part specific to shipping this palette.

##### Status

Web support status lives in `web-platform/reference/browser-compatibility.md`. As of November 2026: `oklch()`, `color-mix()`, `color()`, and `light-dark()` are safe everywhere. Relative color syntax is Baseline (2024-09) and safe for current browsers. `contrast-color()` is Baseline only since 2026-04 and needs a fallback. `dynamic-range-limit` is Chromium only.

WCAG 2.2 is the normative contrast standard. WCAG 3 is a Working Draft whose contrast algorithm "is yet to be determined". It doesn't name APCA.

- [Web: CSS Tokens](#web-css-tokens)

##### Web: CSS Tokens

Names follow `figma-design-system/reference/token-architecture.md`: `--color-primitive-<name>` and `--color-semantic-<group>-<role>`. Primitives and semantics live in one `:root` block. Write primitives in OKLCH, with values from [palette.md](../color-system/palette.md). Semantic tokens reference primitives and switch modes with `light-dark()`, which removes the duplicated dark-mode media query.

```css
:root {
    color-scheme: light dark;   /* required for light-dark() to resolve */

    --color-primitive-swiss-red: oklch(56.71% 0.2067 29.54);
    --color-primitive-bauhaus-red: oklch(54.87% 0.1896 27.76);
    --color-primitive-swiss-red-deep: oklch(49.34% 0.1857 27.49);
    --color-primitive-accent-red-light: oklch(64.93% 0.2141 28.23);
    --color-primitive-accent-red-lighter: oklch(71.05% 0.1777 28.37);
    --color-primitive-accent-red-lightest: oklch(78.11% 0.1239 28.63);
    --color-primitive-swiss-blue: oklch(41.20% 0.1468 262.50);
    --color-primitive-accent-blue-light: oklch(68.42% 0.1609 262.54);
    --color-primitive-swiss-green: oklch(46.78% 0.1091 152.01);
    --color-primitive-accent-green-light: oklch(60.99% 0.1387 151.64);
    --color-primitive-swiss-ochre: oklch(50.91% 0.1037 77.95);
    --color-primitive-swiss-yellow: oklch(84.94% 0.1739 92.82);
    --color-primitive-swiss-ink: oklch(21.78% 0 0);
    --color-primitive-warm-100: oklch(98.43% 0.0040 106.47);
    --color-primitive-warm-200: oklch(96.43% 0.0070 88.64);
    --color-primitive-warm-300: oklch(93.52% 0.0103 81.79);
    --color-primitive-warm-400: oklch(89.06% 0.0138 78.26);
    --color-primitive-warm-700: oklch(51.18% 0.0204 72.87);
    --color-primitive-cool-100: oklch(98.16% 0.0017 247.84);
    --color-primitive-cool-500: oklch(71.08% 0.0098 258.34);
    --color-primitive-cool-700: oklch(43.71% 0.0111 258.36);
    --color-primitive-cool-800: oklch(30.96% 0.0111 271.04);
    --color-primitive-cool-900: oklch(22.60% 0.0083 264.39);
    --color-primitive-cool-950: oklch(17.27% 0.0089 264.31);

    /* Semantic: light value, dark value */
    --color-semantic-background-primary: light-dark(var(--color-primitive-warm-200), var(--color-primitive-cool-900));
    --color-semantic-background-elevated: light-dark(var(--color-primitive-warm-100), var(--color-primitive-cool-800));
    --color-semantic-background-sunken: light-dark(var(--color-primitive-warm-300), var(--color-primitive-cool-950));
    --color-semantic-text-primary: light-dark(var(--color-primitive-swiss-ink), var(--color-primitive-cool-100));
    --color-semantic-text-secondary: light-dark(var(--color-primitive-warm-700), var(--color-primitive-cool-500));
    --color-semantic-text-inverse: light-dark(var(--color-primitive-warm-100), var(--color-primitive-swiss-ink));
    --color-semantic-border-default: light-dark(var(--color-primitive-warm-400), var(--color-primitive-cool-700));
    --color-semantic-interactive-primary: light-dark(var(--color-primitive-swiss-red), var(--color-primitive-accent-red-light));
    --color-semantic-interactive-primary-hover: light-dark(var(--color-primitive-bauhaus-red), var(--color-primitive-accent-red-lighter));
    --color-semantic-interactive-primary-pressed: light-dark(var(--color-primitive-swiss-red-deep), var(--color-primitive-accent-red-lightest));
    --color-semantic-status-error: light-dark(var(--color-primitive-swiss-red-deep), var(--color-primitive-accent-red-light));
    --color-semantic-status-warning: light-dark(var(--color-primitive-swiss-ochre), var(--color-primitive-swiss-yellow));
    --color-semantic-status-success: light-dark(var(--color-primitive-swiss-green), var(--color-primitive-accent-green-light));
    --color-semantic-status-info: light-dark(var(--color-primitive-swiss-blue), var(--color-primitive-accent-blue-light));
    --color-semantic-accent-primary: light-dark(var(--color-primitive-swiss-blue), var(--color-primitive-accent-blue-light));
    --color-semantic-accent-secondary: var(--color-primitive-swiss-yellow);
}

.button {
    background: var(--color-semantic-interactive-primary);
    color: var(--color-semantic-text-inverse);
}
```

A manual theme toggle sets `color-scheme: light` or `color-scheme: dark` on the root, or on any subtree forced to one mode. Every `light-dark()` token below it follows.

##### Deriving States

The palette defines hover and pressed states as named primitives. Use those. When a design calls for a state the palette doesn't name (a tint, a translucent overlay, a focus ring), derive it from a primitive and give the result a token. Don't invent a new literal.

```css
:root {
    /* Relative color: same hue and chroma, adjusted alpha */
    --color-semantic-interactive-primary-subtle: oklch(from var(--color-primitive-swiss-red) l c h / 0.12);

    /* color-mix: blend toward a surface, interpolating in OKLCH */
    --color-semantic-background-tinted: color-mix(in oklch, var(--color-primitive-swiss-red) 8%, var(--color-primitive-warm-200));
}
```

Mix and interpolate in OKLCH or OKLab, not sRGB. sRGB blends of saturated colors pass through muddy, darker midpoints. Same for gradients: `linear-gradient(in oklch, ...)`.

A derived color has a new contrast ratio. Compute it. The parent's ratio doesn't carry over.

##### contrast-color()

`contrast-color(var(--some-fill))` returns `black` or `white`, whichever contrasts more with the input. It's for labels on user-chosen or data-driven fills. For this palette's fixed fills, use the explicit pairings in the contrast tables:

- It only returns pure black or white, not `swiss-ink` or `warm-100`.
- It guarantees the better of the two, not a passing ratio. On mid-tone fills neither option is comfortable, and several of this palette's reds sit there (`swiss-red-warm` gives 4.1:1 with white).
- It's recent, so it needs a declared fallback:

```css
.tag {
    background: var(--tag-color);
    color: var(--color-primitive-swiss-ink);  /* fallback */
    color: contrast-color(var(--tag-color));
}
```

##### Wide Gamut and HDR

Every primitive in this library is inside sRGB and renders identically on sRGB and Display P3 screens. That's deliberate. The palette digitizes printed ink, which is less saturated than a P3 display can show.

A more saturated P3 variant is a new color and a design decision, not a conversion. If I ask for one, keep the primitive's lightness and hue, raise chroma, and scope it to capable displays so sRGB screens keep the original value:

```css
:root {
    --color-primitive-swiss-red: oklch(56.71% 0.2067 29.54);
}

@media (color-gamut: p3) {
    :root {
        --color-primitive-swiss-red: oklch(56.71% 0.24 29.54);   /* example chroma: get the real value from design */
    }
}
```

Raising chroma changes contrast slightly. Recompute. HDR has no role in this palette. Where HDR photography or video sits next to UI in these colors, `dynamic-range-limit` keeps the media from overpowering the interface, but it's Chromium only, so it's an enhancement.

##### Apple: SwiftUI

Define each semantic color as a Color Set in the asset catalog with Any and Dark appearances, then expose it under the shared name. High Contrast variants live in the asset catalog too.

```swift
extension Color {
    enum Semantic {
        enum Background {
            static let primary = Color(.colorSemanticBackgroundPrimary)
        }
        enum Text {
            static let primary = Color(.colorSemanticTextPrimary)
        }
        enum Border {
            static let `default` = Color(.colorSemanticBorderDefault)
        }
        enum Status {
            static let error = Color(.colorSemanticStatusError)
        }
        enum Interactive {
            static let primary = Color(.colorSemanticInteractivePrimary)
            static let primaryHover = Color(.colorSemanticInteractivePrimaryHover)
        }
        enum Accent {
            static let primary = Color(.colorSemanticAccentPrimary)
        }
    }
}

Text("Title")
    .foregroundStyle(Color.Semantic.Text.primary)
    .background(Color.Semantic.Background.primary)
    .border(Color.Semantic.Border.default)
```

`.colorSemanticBackgroundPrimary` is the symbol Xcode generates for a color set of that name. Call sites use the `Color.Semantic` namespace. One nested enum per group: `Background`, `Text`, `Border`, `Status`, `Interactive`, `Accent`. Every role in the mapping table gets a member. `default` needs backticks where it's declared, not where it's used.

Enter the palette's hex values with the color set's color space left at sRGB. They're sRGB values. Tag the same numbers as Display P3 and they render more saturated than specified. Use Display P3 in the asset catalog, or `Color(.displayP3, red:green:blue:opacity:)`, only for a color that was designed in P3.

On Apple platforms the default is the system's semantic colors, which also adapt to Increased Contrast and Liquid Glass. Use this palette for brand and accent roles when a custom palette has been chosen, and leave system backgrounds, labels, and separators to the system unless the design replaces them.

##### Android: Compose

It's a fixed palette or dynamic color, not both. With no style specified, the Android default is dynamic color from the user's wallpaper and this library doesn't apply. When a brand palette is chosen, map the semantic roles onto Material color roles in one place:

```kotlin
private val SwissRed = Color(0xFFD52B1E)
private val SwissInk = Color(0xFF1A1A1A)
private val Warm200 = Color(0xFFF5F3EE)
private val Warm100 = Color(0xFFFAFAF7)
private val Warm400 = Color(0xFFE0DAD1)

val SwissLightColors = lightColorScheme(
    primary = SwissRed,
    onPrimary = Warm100,
    background = Warm200,
    onBackground = SwissInk,
    surface = Warm100,
    onSurface = SwissInk,
    outlineVariant = Warm400
)
```

Material derives many roles this library doesn't define: containers, tertiary, surface tones. Don't leave them at the baseline purple defaults. Map each one deliberately, or generate the full scheme from the chosen primary with Material Theme Builder and pin the roles this library does define.

##### Contrast Standards

WCAG 2 contrast ratios, the numbers in SKILL.md, are the compliance measure. WCAG 2.2 is what laws and procurement rules reference.

APCA is a perceptual contrast model that accounts for font size, weight, and polarity. It was in early WCAG 3 drafts. The current draft leaves the algorithm undecided. It's fine as an extra design check, particularly for dark mode, but an APCA score isn't conformance to anything. A pair still has to meet its WCAG 2 ratio.

Contrast isn't the only requirement. Color is never the sole carrier of meaning (WCAG 1.4.1). Error, warning, and success states need an icon or text alongside the red, yellow, and green.

### From motion-design: Motion Tokens

This is the one definition of the motion token names and their values on every platform. The other files in this skill, and the `apple-platform`, `android-platform`, `web-platform`, and `visual-styles` skills, use these names and don't define their own. Change a value here and nowhere else.

Three families, matching the spring-vs-ease rule. **Spring tokens** for user-triggered motion. **Duration and easing tokens**, used together, for system-triggered motion. A project's design files or existing token set override the values. The names stay. A visual style can declare extra tokens in its own file under the same naming rule. A style-local token is a token, not an inline value.

##### Contents

- [Spring Tokens](#spring-tokens)
- [Duration Tokens](#duration-tokens)
- [Easing Tokens](#easing-tokens)
- [Definitions per Platform](#definitions-per-platform)
- [Reduced Motion Policy](#reduced-motion-policy)
- [Anti-Patterns](#anti-patterns)

##### Spring Tokens

One spring per token, written three ways. All three platforms run the same spring: mass 1, stiffness (2π / duration)², damping ratio 1 - bounce.

| Token | Use | Spring | Swift | Kotlin | CSS |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **snappy** | Press states, toggles, controls | 0.25s, bounce 0.15 | `Motion.Spring.snappy` | `Motion.Spring.snappy()` | `var(--spring-snappy)` over `var(--spring-snappy-duration)` |
| **standard** | Default for interactive elements: cards, sheets, menus, navigation | 0.35s, bounce 0 | `Motion.Spring.standard` | `Motion.Spring.standard()` | `var(--spring-standard)` over `var(--spring-standard-duration)` |
| **expressive** | Visible bounce: FABs, notifications, moments meant to delight | 0.4s, bounce 0.3 | `Motion.Spring.expressive` | `Motion.Spring.expressive()` | `var(--spring-expressive)` over `var(--spring-expressive-duration)` |
| **dragRelease** | An element let go after a drag, settling with the gesture's velocity | 0.3s, bounce 0.28 | `Motion.Spring.dragRelease` | `Motion.Spring.dragRelease()` | none: CSS can't inherit gesture velocity, so drag release on web is driven from JavaScript |

A spring's duration is perceptual, not its settle time. The CSS `--spring-*-duration` values (350ms, 520ms, 660ms) are settle times, which is why they're longer. Each CSS curve is only valid at its paired duration.

Android apps themed with Material 3 Expressive take component and component-like motion from `MaterialTheme.motionScheme` instead. See `android-platform`. `Motion.Spring.*()` is for custom motion the scheme doesn't cover.

##### Duration Tokens

For system-triggered motion, always paired with an easing token. Springs don't take a duration token.

| Token | Value | Use | Swift | Kotlin | CSS |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **micro** | 83ms | Feedback that isn't spring-driven: icon swaps, color flips | `Motion.Duration.micro` | `Motion.Duration.micro` | `var(--duration-micro)` |
| **fast** | 150ms | Small state changes, exits, fades | `Motion.Duration.fast` | `Motion.Duration.fast` | `var(--duration-fast)` |
| **standard** | 250ms | Most transitions: dropdown open, toast appear, content swap | `Motion.Duration.standard` | `Motion.Duration.standard` | `var(--duration-standard)` |
| **slow** | 350ms | Large layout shifts, full-screen transitions | `Motion.Duration.slow` | `Motion.Duration.slow` | `var(--duration-slow)` |
| **cinematic** | 600ms | Deliberate editorial moments, ambient loops | `Motion.Duration.cinematic` | `Motion.Duration.cinematic` | `var(--duration-cinematic)` |

Nothing shorter than **micro**. Below that, make the change instant. Nothing longer than **700ms** in product UI. If an animation needs longer to feel right, more motion isn't the fix. Scroll-scrubbed and ambient WebGL sequences have no duration of their own, so they're exempt.

##### Easing Tokens

| Token | Curve | Use | Swift | Kotlin | CSS |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **enter** | 0, 0, 0.2, 1 | Entrances: decelerates as it arrives | `Motion.Curve.enter` | `Motion.Ease.enter` | `var(--ease-enter)` |
| **exit** | 0.4, 0, 1, 1 | Exits: accelerates as it leaves | `Motion.Curve.exit` | `Motion.Ease.exit` | `var(--ease-exit)` |
| **standard** | 0.4, 0, 0.2, 1 | State changes that stay on screen | `Motion.Curve.standard` | `Motion.Ease.standard` | `var(--ease-standard)` |
| **emphasized** | 0.2, 0, 0, 1 | Quick start, long settle: hero and container moves | `Motion.Curve.emphasized` | `Motion.Ease.emphasized` | `var(--ease-emphasized)` |
| **expo-out** | 0.16, 1, 0.3, 1 | Very fast start, very long tail: reveals | `Motion.Curve.expoOut` | `Motion.Ease.expoOut` | `var(--ease-expo-out)` |
| **sine-in-out** | 0.45, 0.05, 0.55, 0.95 | Gentle and symmetrical: slow, ambient | `Motion.Curve.sineInOut` | `Motion.Ease.sineInOut` | `var(--ease-sine-in-out)` |

Linear isn't a token. It's only right for continuous loops and scroll-linked motion.

Swift is the one exception to the naming rule. SwiftUI animations carry their duration, so `motion/ease/<name>` becomes two things: `Motion.Curve.<name>` is the bare curve, and `Motion.Ease.<name>` is the ready-to-use `Animation`, the curve at its default duration. The pairs are `Motion.Ease.enter` (enter, standard), `exit` (exit, fast), `standard` (standard, standard), `emphasized` (emphasized, slow), `expoOut` (expo-out, cinematic), `fade` (enter, fast), and `ambient` (sine-in-out, cinematic). In Kotlin `Motion.Ease.enter`, `exit`, and `standard` alias Compose's `LinearOutSlowInEasing`, `FastOutLinearInEasing`, and `FastOutSlowInEasing`. Call sites use the token name.

##### Definitions per Platform

One definition site per platform. Call sites reference the token, never a raw curve, duration, or spring constant.

```css
:root {
    --duration-micro: 83ms;
    --duration-fast: 150ms;
    --duration-standard: 250ms;
    --duration-slow: 350ms;
    --duration-cinematic: 600ms;

    --ease-enter: cubic-bezier(0, 0, 0.2, 1);
    --ease-exit: cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 1, 1);
    --ease-standard: cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1);
    --ease-emphasized: cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1);
    --ease-expo-out: cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1);
    --ease-sine-in-out: cubic-bezier(0.45, 0.05, 0.55, 0.95);

    /* Springs as linear() stops: mass 1, stiffness (2π / duration)²,
       damping ratio 1 - bounce, sampled to the point the spring settles
       within 0.1%. */

    /* snappy: duration 0.25s, bounce 0.15 (stiffness 632, damping ratio 0.85) */
    --spring-snappy: linear(0, 0.006 1.2%, 0.026 2.8%, 0.057 4.2%, 0.096 5.8%, 0.191 8.8%, 0.413 15%, 0.514 18%, 0.613 21.2%, 0.698 24.5%, 0.765 27.5%, 0.825 30.8%, 0.873 34%, 0.914 37.5%, 0.946 41.2%, 0.971 45.5%, 0.989 50.2%, 1 55.8%, 1.006 67.8%, 1);
    --spring-snappy-duration: 350ms;

    /* standard: duration 0.35s, bounce 0 (stiffness 322, damping ratio 1) */
    --spring-standard: linear(0, 0.004 1%, 0.019 2.2%, 0.043 3.5%, 0.08 5%, 0.156 7.5%, 0.367 13.8%, 0.463 16.8%, 0.557 20%, 0.638 23.2%, 0.707 26.5%, 0.769 30%, 0.819 33.5%, 0.862 37.2%, 0.901 41.8%, 0.93 46.5%, 0.954 52%, 0.972 58.2%, 0.984 65.2%, 0.992 73.5%, 1);
    --spring-standard-duration: 520ms;

    /* expressive: duration 0.4s, bounce 0.3 (stiffness 247, damping ratio 0.7), 4.6% overshoot */
    --spring-expressive: linear(0, 0.008 1.2%, 0.03 2.5%, 0.063 3.8%, 0.114 5.2%, 0.218 7.8%, 0.476 13.2%, 0.587 15.8%, 0.697 18.5%, 0.783 21%, 0.855 23.5%, 0.918 26.2%, 0.966 29%, 1.003 32%, 1.022 34.2%, 1.036 36.8%, 1.044 39.5%, 1.046 42.5%, 1.041 47.8%, 1.012 62.3%, 1.003 70%, 0.998 81.8%, 1);
    --spring-expressive-duration: 660ms;

    --motion-distance-sm: 12px;
    --motion-distance-md: 24px;
}
```

```swift
import SwiftUI

enum Motion {
    enum Duration {
        static let micro: TimeInterval = 0.083
        static let fast: TimeInterval = 0.15
        static let standard: TimeInterval = 0.25
        static let slow: TimeInterval = 0.35
        static let cinematic: TimeInterval = 0.6
    }

    enum Curve {
        static let enter = UnitCurve.bezier(startControlPoint: UnitPoint(x: 0, y: 0), endControlPoint: UnitPoint(x: 0.2, y: 1))
        static let exit = UnitCurve.bezier(startControlPoint: UnitPoint(x: 0.4, y: 0), endControlPoint: UnitPoint(x: 1, y: 1))
        static let standard = UnitCurve.bezier(startControlPoint: UnitPoint(x: 0.4, y: 0), endControlPoint: UnitPoint(x: 0.2, y: 1))
        static let emphasized = UnitCurve.bezier(startControlPoint: UnitPoint(x: 0.2, y: 0), endControlPoint: UnitPoint(x: 0, y: 1))
        static let expoOut = UnitCurve.bezier(startControlPoint: UnitPoint(x: 0.16, y: 1), endControlPoint: UnitPoint(x: 0.3, y: 1))
        static let sineInOut = UnitCurve.bezier(startControlPoint: UnitPoint(x: 0.45, y: 0.05), endControlPoint: UnitPoint(x: 0.55, y: 0.95))
    }

    enum Spring {
        static let snappy = Animation.snappy(duration: 0.25)                 // bounce 0.15
        static let standard = Animation.spring(duration: 0.35, bounce: 0)
        static let expressive = Animation.spring(duration: 0.4, bounce: 0.3)
        static let dragRelease = Animation.spring(duration: 0.3, bounce: 0.28)
    }

    enum Ease {
        static let enter = Animation.timingCurve(Curve.enter, duration: Duration.standard)
        static let exit = Animation.timingCurve(Curve.exit, duration: Duration.fast)
        static let standard = Animation.timingCurve(Curve.standard, duration: Duration.standard)
        static let emphasized = Animation.timingCurve(Curve.emphasized, duration: Duration.slow)
        static let expoOut = Animation.timingCurve(Curve.expoOut, duration: Duration.cinematic)
        static let fade = Animation.timingCurve(Curve.enter, duration: Duration.fast)
        static let ambient = Animation.timingCurve(Curve.sineInOut, duration: Duration.cinematic)
    }
}
```

```kotlin
import androidx.compose.animation.core.CubicBezierEasing
import androidx.compose.animation.core.Easing
import androidx.compose.animation.core.FastOutLinearInEasing
import androidx.compose.animation.core.FastOutSlowInEasing
import androidx.compose.animation.core.LinearOutSlowInEasing
import androidx.compose.animation.core.SpringSpec
import androidx.compose.animation.core.spring

object Motion {
    object Spring {
        fun <T> snappy(): SpringSpec<T> = spring(dampingRatio = 0.85f, stiffness = 632f)
        fun <T> standard(): SpringSpec<T> = spring(dampingRatio = 1f, stiffness = 322f)
        fun <T> expressive(): SpringSpec<T> = spring(dampingRatio = 0.7f, stiffness = 247f)
        fun <T> dragRelease(): SpringSpec<T> = spring(dampingRatio = 0.72f, stiffness = 439f)
    }

    object Duration {
        const val micro = 83
        const val fast = 150
        const val standard = 250
        const val slow = 350
        const val cinematic = 600
    }

    object Ease {
        val enter: Easing = LinearOutSlowInEasing
        val exit: Easing = FastOutLinearInEasing
        val standard: Easing = FastOutSlowInEasing
        val emphasized: Easing = CubicBezierEasing(0.2f, 0f, 0f, 1f)
        val expoOut: Easing = CubicBezierEasing(0.16f, 1f, 0.3f, 1f)
        val sineInOut: Easing = CubicBezierEasing(0.45f, 0.05f, 0.55f, 0.95f)
    }
}
```

Usage:

```css
.button { transition: scale var(--spring-snappy-duration) var(--spring-snappy); }
.toast  { transition: opacity var(--duration-standard) var(--ease-enter); }
```
```swift
withAnimation(Motion.Spring.standard) { isExpanded.toggle() }
```
```kotlin
animateFloatAsState(target, animationSpec = Motion.Spring.snappy(), label = "scale")
tween<Float>(durationMillis = Motion.Duration.standard, easing = Motion.Ease.enter)
```

GSAP registers the easing tokens under the same names (`"enter"`, `"expo-out"`, and so on). See [gsap.md](../motion-design/gsap.md#setup).

##### Reduced Motion Policy

The policy lives here. Each platform file only shows the API that reads the setting. The reasons are in [foundations.md](../motion-design/foundations.md#why-reduced-motion-matters).

When the user asks for reduced motion:

- **Spatial motion becomes a fade.** Replace slides, zooms, scale, and shared-element travel with an opacity change at **fast** with **enter** (`Motion.Ease.fade`), or an instant change.
- **Springs lose their bounce.** Where a spring stays (a control following a finger), use **standard**, never **expressive**.
- **Scroll-linked motion goes.** No parallax, no scroll-driven transforms, no pinned or scrubbed sequences. Content sits in its final position. Smooth scrolling is off.
- **Autoplaying and looping decoration stops.** A spinner that says "working" can stay.
- **Feedback stays.** Color, opacity, and state changes still happen. Reduced motion never means a control gives no response.

Android's "Remove animations" goes further. It zeroes the animator duration scale, so Compose animations jump to their end state and no substitute fade runs. See [android-compose.md](../motion-design/android-compose.md#reduce-motion).

##### Anti-Patterns

**Linear motion on interactive elements.** Nothing physical moves at constant velocity. Use a spring or an ease.

**Identical timing for all properties.** Opacity that finishes slightly before position reads as one arrival. Opacity that finishes long before it shows the destination before the journey is over.

**Animating layout properties.** `width`, `height`, `top`, `left`, `margin`, `padding` trigger layout every frame. Animate render-time properties: `transform`/`translate`/`scale` and `opacity` on web, `scaleEffect`/`offset` in SwiftUI, `graphicsLayer` in Compose.

**Interrupting without velocity handoff.** When a user reverses direction mid-flight, the new animation has to pick up the current velocity. Springs do. Duration-based animations restart from rest.

**Staggering too much.** 30-60ms between items creates rhythm. 150ms makes the UI feel slow. Stagger the first several items and bring the rest in together.

**Decorative animation on high-frequency paths.** Press feedback is **snappy** or **micro**, nothing longer.

**Parallax on critical content.** It can't be what positions content a user needs to read.

**Inline motion values.** A raw `cubic-bezier()`, a bare millisecond count, or spring constants at a call site.

**Not testing interruption.** Tap, release, tap again rapidly. Swipe, reverse, swipe again. If it breaks, it's duration-based where it should be a spring, or it restarts from a hard-coded start value.

**Skipping reduced motion.** Test every animated surface with the system setting on.

### From motion-design: Web: CSS, Web Animations API & View Transitions

CSS comes first for web motion. `transform`, `opacity`, and `filter` can animate on the compositor and stay smooth while the main thread is busy. GSAP ([gsap.md](../motion-design/gsap.md)) is for timeline choreography, pinning, and text splitting. Nothing else.

Every sample uses the tokens from [cross-platform-tokens.md](../motion-design/cross-platform-tokens.md#definitions-per-platform): `--duration-*`, `--ease-*`, `--spring-*`, `--motion-distance-*`. That `:root` block is the only place a curve or duration literal appears.

##### Status

Support status lives in `web-platform/reference/browser-compatibility.md`. Check it before shipping. What these samples depend on, as of November 2026:

- **Safe everywhere:** `linear()`, individual transform properties, Web Animations API, `@starting-style` entrances, same-document View Transitions.
- **New in one engine, keep the fallback:** scroll-driven animations (Baseline since 2026-10; Firefox only just shipped them).
- **Enhancement only:** animated exits via `display` (no Firefox), `overlay` and `interpolate-size` (Chromium), cross-document View Transitions (no Firefox). The page has to be correct without them, just less animated.

##### Contents

- [Transitions](#transitions)
- [Springs with linear()](#springs-with-linear)
- [Entry and Exit](#entry-and-exit)
- [Animating to Intrinsic Size](#animating-to-intrinsic-size)
- [Web Animations API](#web-animations-api)
- [Scroll-Driven Animations](#scroll-driven-animations)
- [View Transitions](#view-transitions)
- [Reduce Motion (Web)](#reduce-motion-web)

##### Transitions

```css
.reveal {
    opacity: 0;
    translate: 0 var(--motion-distance-md);
    transition:
        translate var(--duration-slow) var(--ease-enter),
        opacity var(--duration-standard) var(--ease-enter);
}
.reveal.visible {
    opacity: 1;
    translate: 0 0;
}
```

The individual `translate`, `scale`, and `rotate` properties composite exactly like `transform` and let each take its own duration and curve.

Don't transition `width`, `height`, `top`, `left`, `margin`, `padding`, or `border-width`. They trigger layout every frame. For layout changes use a View Transition, FLIP ([gsap.md](../motion-design/gsap.md#flip-animations)), or the intrinsic-size techniques below. Don't leave `will-change` on permanently. It holds a layer's memory for as long as it applies, and the browser already promotes an element while it animates.

##### Springs with linear()

CSS has no spring physics, but `linear()` takes any number of stops, so a spring's response can be sampled into one. That's what the `--spring-*` tokens are.

```css
.button {
    transition: scale var(--spring-snappy-duration) var(--spring-snappy);
}
.button:active {
    scale: 0.97;
}
```

Two limits:

- **It's a spring's shape, not a spring.** The curve assumes a start from rest. An interrupted transition restarts from the current value with zero velocity. For taps, hovers, toggles, and menus you can't tell it from a real spring. For drag release, flings, or anything that inherits gesture velocity, compute the spring in JavaScript per frame.
- **A curve is only valid at its paired duration.** Stretch `--spring-expressive` over two seconds and you get a slow wobble, not a softer spring. A different feel is a new token with new spring parameters, defined in the tokens file.

##### Entry and Exit

`@starting-style` gives an element a "before" state the first time it renders or leaves `display: none`, so entrances need no JavaScript.

```css
.toast {
    opacity: 1;
    translate: 0 0;
    transition:
        opacity var(--duration-standard) var(--ease-enter),
        translate var(--duration-standard) var(--ease-enter);

    @starting-style {
        opacity: 0;
        translate: 0 var(--motion-distance-sm);
    }
}
```

Exits need the element to stay rendered until the transition ends. `allow-discrete` lets `display` take part so it flips at the end, and `overlay` keeps a popover or dialog in the top layer meanwhile:

```css
.popover {
    opacity: 0;
    transition:
        opacity var(--duration-fast) var(--ease-exit),
        display var(--duration-fast) allow-discrete,
        overlay var(--duration-fast) allow-discrete;
}
.popover:popover-open {
    opacity: 1;
    transition-timing-function: var(--ease-enter);

    @starting-style {
        opacity: 0;
    }
}
```

Where exits aren't supported the element disappears immediately. That's fine. Don't add JavaScript just to animate an exit.

##### Animating to Intrinsic Size

Opening a disclosure to `height: auto` has no transform equivalent.

```css
/* Works everywhere: animate a grid track from 0fr to 1fr */
.disclosure {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-rows: 0fr;
    transition: grid-template-rows var(--duration-standard) var(--ease-standard);
}
.disclosure[data-open="true"] {
    grid-template-rows: 1fr;
}
.disclosure > .content {
    overflow: hidden;
    min-height: 0;
}

/* Chromium enhancement: lets height transition to and from auto */
:root {
    interpolate-size: allow-keywords;
}
```

Both animate layout, so keep them to small regions.

##### Web Animations API

When JavaScript has to start, reverse, seek, or await an animation, use `element.animate()` before a library. It runs the same compositor-backed animations and reads the same tokens.

```javascript
const rootStyle = getComputedStyle(document.documentElement);
const token = (name) => rootStyle.getPropertyValue(name).trim();

async function dismiss(card) {
    const animation = card.animate(
        { opacity: [1, 0], translate: ["0 0", `0 ${token("--motion-distance-sm")}`] },
        {
            duration: parseFloat(token("--duration-fast")),
            easing: token("--ease-exit"),
            fill: "forwards"
        }
    );
    await animation.finished;
    card.remove();
}
```

`reverse()`, `playbackRate`, and `currentTime` cover interruption and scrubbing. If the element stays in the DOM, call `commitStyles()` then `cancel()`. Don't leave a `fill: "forwards"` animation holding styles.

##### Scroll-Driven Animations

No JavaScript, and `transform`/`opacity` keyframes run on the compositor. Use them for scroll progress, reveal-on-enter, and single-element parallax. Move to GSAP ScrollTrigger when a section has to pin or one scrubbed timeline choreographs many elements.

The timing function is `linear` on purpose: scroll position is the clock. Shape the motion with keyframe offsets and `animation-range`.

```css
/* Scroll progress timeline: tied to a scroll container's position */
.progress-bar {
    transform-origin: left;
    animation: grow linear both;
    animation-timeline: scroll(root block);   /* after the shorthand, which resets it */
}
@keyframes grow {
    from { scale: 0 1; }
    to   { scale: 1 1; }
}

/* View timeline: tied to the element's own visibility in the scrollport */
.section-reveal {
    animation: reveal linear both;
    animation-timeline: view();
    animation-range: entry 0% cover 40%;
}
@keyframes reveal {
    from { opacity: 0; translate: 0 var(--motion-distance-md); }
    to   { opacity: 1; translate: 0 0; }
}

/* Named timeline: several elements driven by one scroller */
.scroll-container {
    scroll-timeline: --hero-scroll block;
}
.hero-text {
    animation: fade-out linear both;
    animation-timeline: --hero-scroll;
    animation-range: 0% 30%;
}
@keyframes fade-out {
    to { opacity: 0; }
}
```

For the fallback, ship a base state driven by a class from `IntersectionObserver` and upgrade inside `@supports`.

```css
.animated-element {
    opacity: 0;
    translate: 0 var(--motion-distance-md);
    transition:
        opacity var(--duration-slow) var(--ease-enter),
        translate var(--duration-slow) var(--ease-enter);
}
.animated-element.visible {
    opacity: 1;
    translate: 0 0;
}

@supports (animation-timeline: view()) {
    .animated-element {
        transition: none;
        animation: reveal linear both;
        animation-timeline: view();
        animation-range: entry 0% entry 60%;
    }
}
```

##### View Transitions

Same-document transitions start from JavaScript. Cross-document transitions are declared in CSS for multi-page sites. A browser without support just navigates normally.

```javascript
function navigateTo(url) {
    if (!document.startViewTransition) {
        return loadPage(url);
    }
    return document.startViewTransition(() => loadPage(url)).finished;
}
```

```css
/* The default is a root cross-fade. Name an element to morph it between states. */
.hero-image {
    view-transition-name: hero;
}

::view-transition-group(hero) {
    animation-duration: var(--duration-slow);
    animation-timing-function: var(--ease-emphasized);
}
::view-transition-old(root) {
    animation: var(--duration-fast) var(--ease-exit) both fade-out;
}
::view-transition-new(root) {
    animation: var(--duration-standard) var(--ease-enter) both fade-in;
}

@keyframes fade-out { to { opacity: 0; } }
@keyframes fade-in { from { opacity: 0; } }
```

A `view-transition-name` has to be unique among rendered elements at capture time. Two elements sharing one aborts the transition. For lists, give each item its own name with an inline style and style them as a group with `view-transition-class`.

Cross-document:

```css
/* In the CSS of every page that should participate */
@view-transition {
    navigation: auto;
}
```

Both documents have to opt in. The transition only runs for a same-origin navigation with no cross-origin redirect. Back and forward qualify. A new navigation qualifies only when it starts from the page (link, form, script), not from browser UI like the address bar. Reloads never transition. Names and pseudo-elements work exactly as above.

##### Reduce Motion (Web)

The policy is in [cross-platform-tokens.md](../motion-design/cross-platform-tokens.md#reduced-motion-policy). In CSS, write spatial motion as an opt-in for users who haven't asked for less. The fade stays for everyone.

```css
.reveal {
    opacity: 0;
    transition: opacity var(--duration-fast) var(--ease-enter);
}
.reveal.visible {
    opacity: 1;
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
    .reveal {
        translate: 0 var(--motion-distance-md);
        transition:
            translate var(--duration-slow) var(--ease-enter),
            opacity var(--duration-standard) var(--ease-enter);
    }
    .reveal.visible {
        translate: 0 0;
    }
}

/* Scroll-linked motion and View Transition movement are removed outright */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
    .parallax,
    .section-reveal {
        animation: none;
        opacity: 1;
        translate: none;
    }

    ::view-transition-group(*),
    ::view-transition-old(*),
    ::view-transition-new(*) {
        animation: none;
    }

    html {
        scroll-behavior: auto;
    }
}
```

The global reset (`* { animation-duration: 0.01ms !important; ... }`) kills fades and spinners too. Scope it to third-party markup you don't control. It isn't the primary mechanism.

In JavaScript, `window.matchMedia("(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)")` gives the same answer. Listen for its `change` event, because the user can flip the setting while the page is open. GSAP doesn't read the preference on its own ([gsap.md](../motion-design/gsap.md#reduced-motion)). Lenis does by default.
